title: Rahul Gandhi: India bloc leaders march to Supreme Court as protests continue
description: India's opposition parties are marching to the Supreme Court in Delhi to demand the resignation of the election chief over alleged voter fraud.  This
body: India's opposition parties are marching to the Supreme Court in Delhi to demand the resignation of the election chief over alleged voter fraud.  This will be the latest in a series of demonstrations in Delhi, with thousands of security forces deployed and roads barricaded in the capital.Attempts to hold a protest by the Cockroach Janata Party pressure group over the weekend led to thousands of demonstrators being detained.Opposition parties allege that under Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, India's voter rolls are being manipulated to benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). Both the Election Commission and the BJP have rejected the charge.The opposition lawmakers want to submit a memorandum to Chief Justice Surya Kant, but he has told reporters he declined the meeting citing "certain reasons".He did not provide the reasons, but media reports citing the letter have said that he pointed out that some of the issues the opposition wanted to raise with him were also pending before the court. The BBC has not seen the letter."Every Indian citizen has the right to approach the court, and we will hear their concerns and grant whatever is due under the law," he told reporters.Congress MP Rahul Gandhi, meanwhile, has called "all opposition parties, civil society groups [and] all those who believe in democracy" to join Monday's march.In a press conference on Monday, he shared a letter that he and Congress President Mallikarjun Kharge had written to the Chief Justice, laying out their concerns with Kumar's alleged conduct and with the contentious electoral roll revision.He said that Kant had asked them to file a petition, which they would do at the end of their march.Authorities in Delhi have announced heavy restrictions on traffic and on entry and exit at some key metro stations. There is also heavy security deployment in central Delhi and along the route of the march.Several thousand people were on Barakhamba road, where the march began, as a bus carrying Rahul Gandhi and other opposition leaders arrived just before 15:30 local time. Supporters waved flags and chanted his name as the Congress MP and others waved through the windows. Seated a few rows behind Rahul was Neha Bora, a leftist student leader who has gained prominence for participating in the protests.Over the past week, top opposition leaders, including Rahul Gandhi, have been briefly detained several times while leading protests in central Delhi.On Sunday, the CJP - which is not a registered political party - said it would continue protesting until Kumar stepped down.The CJP, which successfully led a protest over the summer that culminated in India's federal education minister's resignation, had called for a march on Saturday to Jantar Mantar - the best-known protest site in Delhi where the last set of sit-in demonstrations had also happened.But authorities in Delhi imposed overarching restrictions that made it almost impossible for protesters to travel and reach Jantar Mantar - trains were cancelled, dozens of metro stations were shut down and tens of thousands of police and paramilitary personnel were on the roads to detain protesters.The CJP leaders - founder Abhijeet Dipke and co-convenors Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka - were dramatically detained from a plane as they landed in Delhi to join the protest. They were only released a day later - while Dipke has returned home to attend his grandmother's funeral, Das and Ranka held a press conference where they said the protests would continue. Both leaders, however, did not join the protests on Sunday but have said they will seek a new protest date from the police.Over the weekend, the police detained and released thousands of people, including several journalists. Some videos and photos from the protest show police dragging people, including women, by force and pushing them into buses.The BBC also captured visuals, external of a policeman slapping a detained protester inside a bus. The Delhi Police did not respond to questions about the use of violence against protesters.In a statement, Reporters Without Borders condemned the detention of at least 16 Indian journalists."Covering events of public interest is not a crime. It is their job. The police's actions against the press are unacceptable," it said.Congress leader Gandhi said that young Indians who had come to peacefully protest with "love in their hearts, not hatred or anger" had been beaten up.BJP President Nitin Nabin accused opposition parties and the CJP of trying to destabilise India "at the behest of foreign forces" without elaborating on who the forces were.

schema.headline: Rahul Gandhi: India bloc leaders march to Supreme Court as protests continue

title: Poland stabbings driven by online glorification of violence, Tusk says
description: Three violent attacks at Polish schools this week were driven by the "glorification of violence" online, Prime Minister Donald Tusk said.The attacks h
body: Three violent attacks at Polish schools this week were driven by the "glorification of violence" online, Prime Minister Donald Tusk said.The attacks have left one woman dead and others injured, including children."These are very often spontaneous actions inspired by online activity," Tusk said on Sunday, during a crisis meeting with security services. Police have arrested 117 people across the country for possession knives or other weapons, or for threatening to attack schools or fellow students, after searching tens of thousands of schools.A woman was arrested on Saturday after injuring three people while attacking a 17-year-old girl at an educational institution in the capital, Warsaw.It came a day after thousands of police visited schools across Poland, following two stabbing attacks earlier in the week, one of which led to the killing of a female caretaker."We are not dealing with any group organized on a big scale," Tusk said on Sunday. "In the past years and months, we have noted - globally and in Poland - a rise in the fascination with violence," he added.The prime minister said the attacks were acts of "nihilistic violence" associated with the extreme right."Some of the people detained are active in the ultraright environment," he said, adding that police had noticed a rise in online searches of Nazi content as well as of "mass killers who have become idols online".On Wednesday, a 19-year-old student attacked and injured nine people at a vocational school in the central Polish province of Mazovian.A day later, the 37-year-old caretaker was killed after a 15-year-old entered a primary school in Leszczydół-Nowiny, north of Warsaw.Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński also said a 17-year-old was detained in the town of Sierpc, north-west of Warsaw, after allegedly stating "on school grounds that he planned to do something... dangerous - that he intended to harm someone".Thousands of Polish ‌police officers visited schools nationwide to try to reassure pupils after the stabbings sparked rumours of a "Bloody Friday" of more attacks stemming from a supposed online challenge.Meanwhile, Polish security services convened a special meeting on Sunday after receiving information about a potential attack on Tusk and Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz, a spokesperson said.A special services spokesman said officials were treating the threat as "deadly serious".

schema.headline: Poland stabbings driven by online glorification of violence, Tusk says

title: Trump faces growing backlash over plans to import diesel from Russia
description: US President Donald Trump is facing a growing backlash over plans to import diesel from Russia as the Iran war continues to impact global energy price
body: US President Donald Trump is facing a growing backlash over plans to import diesel from Russia as the Iran war continues to impact global energy prices.Trump on Friday announced that Russian President Vladimir Putin had agreed to release 300,000 tonnes of diesel immediately "to the American and global marketplace" followed by several other shipments. That is despite signing legislation to authorise fresh US sanctions and tariffs on nations that import Russian oil and gas just weeks ago.The move has been criticised by some Republican and Democratic lawmakers, who believe the deal violates US laws.As well as the initial release of 300,000 tonnes of diesel, Trump said Russia would then supply 500,000 tonnes in November and one million more after that.This would be followed by a further three million tonnes, which would be delivered "within a short period" dependent on the condition of its refineries, which have been attacked by Ukraine during the ongoing war between the two countries."Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority," Trump wrote in a Truth Social post.Russia's Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak confirmed these numbers to Tass, the country's state-owned news agency, saying the export volume could reach three million tonnes per month in future.Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has called the deal a gift to Putin that amounts to "an investment in a war that must be ended". It is understood the US Treasury is suspending sanctions on Russian diesel exports until 7 April as part of the deal, but other assets like those in American banks are still frozen.A group of seven senators - four Republicans and three Democrats – on Sunday said the deal violated US laws, urging Trump to "reverse course"."The United States should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians," the lawmakers said.They added that Congress had "explicitly banned Russian energy imports in 2022 to prevent American dollars from financing Putin's brutal war against Ukraine". The statement was signed by Republicans Susan Collins, Lisa Murkowski, Thom Tillis and John Curtis, as well as Democrats Jeanne Shaheen, Richard Blumenthal and Ron Wyden.Not everyone is opposed to the deal. Republican Thomas Massie, who has sparred with Trump a number of issues, said the US should lift sanctions on all petroleum products.Trump's Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Fox News the agreement would work through existing legal channels the US has to help bring prices down and that anyone in Congress who said it would not was wrong. Global fuel prices have soared since the US-Israel war with Iran began at the end of February, with the fighting severely disrupting supplies of crude oil - a key ingredient in petrol and diesel. The rising prices have become a key issue for Americans ahead of next month's midterms elections, which will determine if Trump's Republican Party maintains control of Congress.Polls show a majority of Americans disapprove of his handling of the economy and the war in Iran and he has been searching for ways to ease his party's political pain.The toll the war is taking has been acutely felt by US agricultural states, which rely heavily on diesel to operate farming machinery and to transport their products to market.The average diesel price in the US is currently $6.28 (£4.74) a gallon, according to the AAA, down from the record high of $6.53 recorded at the end of September.Analysts have questioned whether Russia is capable of providing that quantity of diesel and the extent to which doing so will ease prices for American consumers.The US uses approximately 3.6 million barrels of diesel a day, so even if Russia delivers its promised 300,000 tonnes this month, it amounts to approximately half of the US daily consumption.It is not only at home that Trump is facing opposition to his diesel deal with Russia. A number of international leaders have criticised it, including Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting, who said the US and other allies of Ukraine should focus on ramping up pressure on Russia to end the war. Meanwhile, Trump announced in Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had reached an "energy ceasefire" but did not give more details. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky welcomed this but there was no response from Moscow.

schema.headline: Trump faces growing backlash over plans to import diesel from Russia

title: Robert Pattinson on new film Primetime and how hunting predators became hit TV
description: Robert Pattinson is having quite the year.The British actor has already starred opposite Zendaya in The Drama, and played a key role in summer blockbu
body: Robert Pattinson is having quite the year.The British actor has already starred opposite Zendaya in The Drama, and played a key role in summer blockbuster The Odyssey.But his new film, Primetime, takes him in a completely new direction - as he portrays the real-life host of American TV show, To Catch a Predator.The show, which aired from 2004 to 2007, involved hunting alleged child abusers.For Pattinson, who became a father almost three years ago, the film's plot is particularly concerning."It's both the most terrifying thing that can happen to you, whether you're a parent, or even if you're not," he told BBC News at the film's screening at London Film Festival."It's the most unimaginable sin possible," he added.Robert Pattinson: Being a dad makes life 'more fun'The new A24 crime thriller depicts the show's host, NBC journalist Chris Hansen, carrying out sting operations on would-be predators.The show was a ratings hit.But it also led to questions over where to draw the line between investigative journalism, police activity and reality television.Speaking on Sunday night, Pattinson reflected on the show's complicated legacy."The show was this kind of microcosm of saying, 'oh, we can do something about [child abuse], and we can do something about it really, really, really quickly," he said."And in some ways, that's correct, but it also makes for incredibly powerful TV, and that's when it gets into slightly dicey territory."Pattinson, 40, became something of a pin-up after playing vampire Edward Cullen in the Twilight series, alongside American actress Kristen Stewart.Before that, he stole young hearts as Hufflepuff hunk Cedric Diggory in Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire.He has since starred in major films including Christopher Nolan's Tenet, as well as a range of eccentric, indie films.This year, he has been on a roll, with Dune: Part Three still to come.He’s also got the next Batman film in the pipeline, although production on that has reportedly paused, external. When asked when they'll be back to work, Pattinson didn’t give much away ("We don't know yet, but yeah, working on it.")Primetime has also led to speculation that this could be the year that Pattinson gets his first ever Oscars nomination. Is that likely, I wonder?"I am eternally grateful that I got these jobs," he responds."But then [to have] been able to even do them, this is one of the best years of my life."

schema.headline: Robert Pattinson on new film Primetime and how hunting predators became hit TV

title: Riyadh airport attacks another dangerous moment in already tense conflict
description: Image source, EPA/ShutterstockImage caption, Houthi soldiers stand guard during a protest against Saudi Arabia, in Sana'a, Yemen,  on FridayByFrank Ga
body: Image source, EPA/ShutterstockImage caption, Houthi soldiers stand guard during a protest against Saudi Arabia, in Sana'a, Yemen,  on FridayByFrank GardnerBBC security correspondent and Jon DonnisonReporting fromJerusalemThe attacks on King Khalid Airport in Riyadh mark another dangerous moment in a region that is already fraught with tension and conflict.Saudi Arabia wasn't ready for this. In recent weeks the Houthis have stepped up their attacks on Saudi Arabian soil, but their attacks over the past few days have hit the country's critical infrastructure in the form of the capital's main airport, apparently penetrating Saudi air defences with ease.Saturday's attack killed 12 people and hurt more than 300. On Sunday the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said an "unknown projectile" had hit a passenger hall and a cruise missile had been intercepted nearby.The physical damage can be quickly repaired, but the country's reputation as a safe haven of stability is taking a battering.As well as all the airport attacks, the Houthis have sought to take control of strategically significant positions along the Red Sea coast and around the Bab al-Mandeb Strait. This further increases the risk to safe navigation along the vital maritime corridor - although the Yemeni government says it has "secured" the strait.The civil war in Yemen between the country's government - which is internationally recognised and supported by Saudi Arabia - and the Houthis, who are backed by Iran, has been going on for more than a decade. It has left many thousands of people dead and plunged Yemen into one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.It is a complex and often confusing geopolitical conflict, and this latest escalation needs to be seen in the broader context of the tension between Iran, the United States and Israel.Not since the al-Qaeda insurgency of the mid-2000s has the Kingdom faced such a serious threat. The Saudi government overcame that challenge through an effective hearts and minds campaign. Then it weathered the Arab Spring uprisings around the region which saw off leaders in Tunisia, Libya, Egypt and Yemen. It even shrugged off – with some annoyance – an Iranian ballistic missile attack on Riyadh in March.But this is different. Saudi Arabia may have one of the most powerful air forces in the Middle East, and it has been carrying out devastating air strikes on Houthi positions. Despite this, the opposing forces have managed to seize large portions of the country, particularly in the north and west.But the Houthis know exactly where to hit back: at the soft underbelly of the Saudi economy.As part of the "axis of resistance", the Houthis are a vital strategic partner for Iran. From Jizan on the Red Sea to the petrochemical complex at Khurais, the Houthis are delivering explosive drones and missiles with deadly accuracy.The Red Sea shipping route has become increasingly important, because the Strait of Hormuz, on the other side of the Gulf, has still not fully reopened since the US and Iran have failed to reach a deal to end their war.Targeting ships in the Red Sea is another way that the Houthis are trying to exert leverage - the attacks cause global economic damage, which is a key bargaining chip for Tehran.In early September, the White House stated it would not directly intervene in the Yemen conflict, but could provide intelligence support to the Saudis. It later confirmed that it was supplying intelligence and had deployed military experts to Saudi Arabia.However the situation may have taken a new turn following the latest attack on Riyadh, which killed a US citizen.Speaking to reporters, US President Donald Trump called Saturday's attack "terrible" and indicated he may intervene militarily with the Saudis. "We just found out about the recent attack, so we'll make a decision. We move very quickly," Trump said.But that now seems unlikely, at least before crucial US midterm elections next month.When he was re-elected in 2024, Trump promised to end America's role in wars around the world. Despite this, the US is currently involved in three unresolved conflicts in the Middle East - in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.Should Trump get embroiled in another one, this time in Yemen, it is unlikely to go down well with voters.This war now looks like it will intensify before it ends in another shaky truce - with or without US involvement.Additional analysis from Abdelbassir Hassan, BBC Arabic

schema.headline: Riyadh airport attacks another dangerous moment in already tense conflict

title: Kenyan mourners killed by police at Raila Odinga memorial not involved in violence, BBC Africa Eye finds
description: Three mourners killed when Kenyan police opened fire at a national farewell for former Prime Minister Raila Odinga were not involved in a clash that s
body: Three mourners killed when Kenyan police opened fire at a national farewell for former Prime Minister Raila Odinga were not involved in a clash that sparked gunfire, a BBC Africa Eye investigation has found.During an event held last October for people to pay their respects to Odinga, three people were shot dead after mourners attempted to gain access to the VIP section of Nairobi's Kasarani Stadium by force.BBC analysis from inside the stadium shows the victims were each between at least 60m (197 ft) and 160m from the scuffles.Kenya's Interior Minister Kipchumba Murkomen told the BBC that the police action had been "restrained" after the crowd starting throwing stones.In footage analysed by the BBC, it is clear that objects, including plastic chairs, are thrown, but we have no evidence that they included stones.The BBC went through more than 1,500 images and videos to establish the location of those killed in the stadium on 16 October 2025, and also spoke to some of their relatives.Forensic analysis by the BBC suggests an elite police unit responsible for protecting the president may have fired the fatal shots.Kenya's longest serving opposition leader and former prime minister died the previous day while receiving medical treatment in India. He was one of the country's most influential political figures.A year on, Kenya's police watchdog, the Independent Policing Oversight Authority (IPOA), is still investigating the deaths and police response and no-one has been held to account.The interior minister defended the police by saying they had been under "so much pressure" after working for many hours non-stop and had been deployed to a new venue at the last minute."The investigations are being done by an independent police oversight authority, we believe that their findings will help us take appropriate legal action," Murkomen said.Responding to questions about the conduct of police he said: "I don't think… somebody [was] sitting there and saying: 'Shoot now'. It is the judgment of the police officer at the spur of the moment."Yvonne Akinyi, who husband was among those killed told the BBC: "The people who we look at to protect us, these are the people that cause us this pain. These are the people that make us to become young widows in this country, young orphans in this county," she said.Odinga's death at 80 prompted an outpouring of grief across Kenya. Thousands gathered at Nairobi's Jomo Kenyatta International Airport as his body was flown home.The body had originally been due to lie in state at parliament, but the scale of the crowds and fears of a security breach forced a last-minute change of venue to Kasarani Stadium. Officials say they had little time to secure the 48,000-capacity venue, and thousands spilled onto the pitch and into the stands unchecked.After several hours of waiting to see the coffin in 30C heat with no public address system for official updates, a small section of the crowd began throwing objects, including plastic chairs, at officers guarding the VIP pavilion. Police fired live rounds as mourners pushed toward the pavilion. Footage from elsewhere in the stadium shows the crowd remained largely peaceful.Autopsy reports confirm that Ogutu died from a gunshot wound to the chest and 42 year-old Burka was fatally shot in the head.Piecing together a timeline of events, BBC Africa Eye identified at least eight police officers operating together, wearing tactical clothing and military camouflage. These officers carry assault rifles, with no visible insignia and faces covered.Their uniforms and movements are consistent with a layer of security assigned to President William Ruto and other VIPs before and after the shooting. At least three officers of this unit appear to fire their weapons. The BBC identified three of them as part of an elite police unit responsible for presidential protection. The BBC cannot establish which bullets killed each victim, and cannot rule out other officers firing inside the stadium.Kenya's National Police Service told the BBC: "There are huge lessons picked from the day's events," which had "formed a fundamental learning curve for a better, more professional application in the future." The IPOA did not respond to a request for comment.

schema.headline: Kenyan mourners killed by police at Raila Odinga memorial not involved in violence, BBC Africa Eye finds

title: Deloitte helped in falsifying documents to evade tax on Abramovich’s wealth, BBC finds
description: The world's biggest accountancy firm helped in falsifying documents to hide Roman Abramovich's wealth and evade tax, BBC Panorama has found.Accounts s
body: The world's biggest accountancy firm helped in falsifying documents to hide Roman Abramovich's wealth and evade tax, BBC Panorama has found.Accounts signed off by Deloitte in Cyprus meant assets such as superyachts, mansions and private jets worth $672m (£508m) vanished from Abramovich's company accounts.Deloitte also appears to have advised on a scheme to evade a huge tax bill on the oligarch's wealth through the falsification of documents.Barrister Andrew Mitchell KC, an expert in financial services law, said Panorama's evidence showed the scheme was "straightforward" tax evasion and "it couldn't be more blatant".Roman Abramovich's lawyers said he denies that he evaded tax or concealed his fortune. They said Panorama provided no evidence he knew about, authorised or directed the falsification of any document and said it was legitimate to rely on advice from professionals.Deloitte Cyprus said it "acts in compliance with applicable laws".The findings are being revealed following a joint investigation between BBC Panorama and the Bureau of Investigative Journalism. For nearly two decades, Roman Abramovich was the most famous Russian oligarch in the UK, welcomed in London where he bought Chelsea Football Club in 2003 and bankrolled the club's most successful period. But after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, he was sanctioned by the UK government as an associate of President Vladimir Putin and forced to sell the club.Abramovich has been reported to be living in Turkey, a safe haven for him because it did not apply sanctions. In the Channel Island of Jersey, £5.4bn of his assets remain frozen and a criminal investigation has been going on for four years.The oligarch's lawyers told the BBC he denies the allegations in the Jersey investigation and says it was "undertaken for political purposes".Our investigation has uncovered new evidence about the way Abramovich's business empire has been run. It also raises serious questions about the integrity of some of his professional advisers.Lord Sikka, professor of accounting at the University of Sheffield, said it was a "violation of a statutory duty" and "pretty scandalous" to misrepresent transaction dates and not to publish true and fair accounts.Panorama also found evidence that backdated documents had been used in a tax evasion scheme.This involved another one of Abramovich's Cypriot companies, Kravin Investments, which had almost $2bn in the bank in 2003.It had been earning large amounts in interest, so Roman Abramovich's company should have been paying tax on that interest to the Cypriot authorities.But his advisers had another idea to rewrite history.An email from MeritServus in August 2005 to Abramovich's Russian associates said a plan had been devised after a meeting with Deloitte. "If you agree, it will be necessary to change the financial statements and the accounting records accordingly for 2003 and 2004," the email read.MeritServus informed the oligarch's Russian associates, that Kravin's "Provisional Tax Assessments for 2005" would be filed showing the company earning no income from the money.A month later, an associate in Russia emailed in response, "I agree". MeritServus then created a series of backdated documents which falsely purported to show that Kravin was only holding and investing the funds on behalf of its parent company in the BVI.This made it look like Kravin did not actually own the money, so it would not be liable for tax in Cyprus.Deloitte wrote in a September 2005 email that "certain changes will have to be made to the accounts (bank account balances, interest income, profit and loss account)" because of the backdated changes to Kravin's assets.So Deloitte was apparently advising on the falsification of financial records. The evidence suggests it allowed Abramovich's company to evade millions in tax.Andrew Mitchell KC told us the scheme was "straightforward" tax evasion. "If it happened in England and it was in the millions, His Majesty's Revenue and Customs would be thinking about a prosecution," he said.Cypriot MP Christos Christofides said that if tax had been evaded, then "we have to see how we can get our money back and how, if some people are guilty, they have to pay the price according to our law."In addition to the documents which Deloitte helped to backdate, Abramovich's advisers at MeritServus falsified a third set of records. This involved the oligarch's huge business fortune - more than $10bn - held by a company called Electus Investments in Cyprus.MeritServus backdated documents to make it look like Electus did not own the fortune.It used another Abramovich company with exactly the same name of Electus Investments, but this time based in the more secretive BVI, where accounts did not have to be made public.Emails show that in 2006, MeritServus acknowledged that the fortune was owned by Electus Cyprus. But again it proposed to rewrite the past, this time "to transfer the beneficial ownership to Electus Investments in the BVI" and make it look as though the change had happened three years earlier.MeritServus signed and backdated documents which falsely purported to show the BVI company had owned the $10bn fortune since 20 November 2003. So when the accounts of the Cypriot company with the same name were made public, it appeared to have assets worth just $145,000.Roman Abramovich's billions had been made to disappear.

schema.headline: Deloitte helped in falsifying documents to evade tax on Abramovich’s wealth, BBC finds

title: Women's football: Billion-dollar boom is leaving players behind - Fifpro raises concerns
description: Women's football is on course to become a billion-dollar industry, but many professional players are still earning low wages, working on insecure cont
body: Women's football is on course to become a billion-dollar industry, but many professional players are still earning low wages, working on insecure contracts and experiencing rising psychological stress.That is according to the findings of a new global survey of more than 800 footballers by the players' union Fifpro., externalPlayers were asked why they might leave football early. The report stated 59% cited financial reasons, while psychological stress was another factor identified by 46%. Alex Culvin, head of women's football at Fifpro, said there was no single explanation for the increase. She pointed to growing public exposure, financial insecurity and inadequate support systems as possible contributing factors."Players are now very visible," she said."Players are not only expected to be visible, but are obligated to be visible because of the low income to subsidise the lack of solid income they receive."While awareness of mental health issues has improved, Culvin explained many players felt they were being left to cope alone."Players also reported, whilst having a higher psychological stress, that they didn't have the support they needed in a mental health sense, either at the club or internationally," she said.In total, the report shows 57% of women who responded to the survey struggled with their mental health and half of them were not provided with support by their clubs.One of the report's most striking findings is how players view their own professional status.Under Fifa's definition, a professional player has a written contract and is paid more than the expenses incurred playing.In the survey, 62% of players described themselves as professional, 27% selected semi-professional and 12% chose amateur.All players in the survey were playing for clubs in the top tier of their country, yet only 78% reported having a written contract and 82% said they were paid by their club.However, just 57% said that payment was enough to cover the costs of playing football."Players who are professional but don't see or feel themselves as professional are not receiving the full benefits of being an employee," Culvin said.The report also highlights the limits of salary growth. Although mean average monthly earnings have tripled since 2017 to $2,601 (£1,970), the median salary is just $1,669 (£1,250).Average monthly pay varies considerably by region, from $6,450 (£4,886) in North America and $3,982 (£3,016) in central/Western Europe, to $878 (£664) in Eastern Europe and just $480 (£363) in Africa.While salaries have risen sharply in leagues such as those in the USA and Mexico, average pay in 10 Eastern European countries remains below the national minimum wage.Even in regions such as Western Europe and Asia/Oceania that span some bigger football markets, average pay is not significantly higher than national minimum wage levels.Fifpro was unable to provide average salaries per league as the report focused on regions rather than individual countries.Average contract lengths have also increased from about one year in 2017 to 19 months, but many players still face periods without guaranteed income."Only two-thirds of players are paid for the whole 12 months," said Culvin."There's a lot of players who are on seven-month contracts, nine-month contracts, which means that they've got to work to make up the rest of the calendar year."She believes the rapid commercial growth of women's football has helped to obscure some of these realities.Despite the rapid growth of England's Women's Super League, Fifpro says conditions at the top of the game could obscure the reality for many players elsewhere.Culvin warned the economic boom in women's football could "mask some of the realities that players face and actually endure on a day-to-day basis".The report also found that 24% of players had experienced late payments over the past two seasons, while 42% were not provided with a pension.Culvin argues there is a growing disconnect between expectations and reality."I think there's a wake-up call needed for the ecosystem, that our players are suffering and that there is not the kind of wraparound support and accountability that's needed for players," she said.However, not all trends were negative.One significant improvement being felt in the game concerns parenthood.In 2017, nearly half of respondents considering leaving the game early said wanting a family could drive them out of football.That figure has now fallen to 19%, which Fifpro attributes in part to maternity regulations that were introduced by Fifa in 2021 and updated two years ago."What we've concluded, which I think is incredibly important, is that targeted regulatory intervention works - maternity regulations were introduced in 2021," said Culvin.The report highlights a widening divide within the women's game. The sport's elite clubs and players have benefited from investment and visibility, yet much of the global workforce remains vulnerable."You've got an industry that's very focused on the top 5% of players," Culvin said."But then what you've got is the rest, which is 95% of the industry who are not paid on time, who have short contracts. They don't get paid for 12 months - they are in incredibly vulnerable and precarious environments."Despite that, Fifpro insists the solution is not to slow down growth but to ensure that commercial success and player welfare develop together."There doesn't need to be a choice for those between commercial growth and player protection," said Culvin."Those two things need to go hand in hand and work in tandem."Her conclusion is clear."What we're saying is enough is enough and the industry needs to react to the players' needs and centralise the players' voice, ensure that players have a seat at the table when decisions that affect them are being made about them."

schema.headline: Women's football: Billion-dollar boom is leaving players behind - Fifpro raises concerns

title: Pope Leo XIV to have surgery after nodule found on lung
description: Pope Leo XIV has announced he will be operated on "in the coming days" after a nodule was found on his lung during a medical check-up."The doctors fou
body: Pope Leo XIV has announced he will be operated on "in the coming days" after a nodule was found on his lung during a medical check-up."The doctors found an early, well-localised nodule on my lung," he told the public during his weekly Sunday prayers in St Peter's Square in Rome.The 71-year-old said his medical team "believe it would be right to intervene" and he had agreed to the operation, while reassuring pilgrims that the mass was "well-contained" and caught "at an early stage".The pontiff's admission that he would need surgery comes nearly a year-and-a-half after he succeeded the late Pope Francis, who also experienced issues with his lungs that required hospital treatment.Leo concluded his Angelus prayer by thanking everyone for their "spiritual closeness" and said he entrusted himself to their prayers.Holy See Press Office spokesman Matteo Bruni told the media that "the operation is scheduled for the first days of next week".He added that the Pope is expected to take about a week to recover.Vatican News, the Holy See's news portal, said the operation will take place at Gemelli Hospital in Rome.The hospital set up a special Papal suite following the failed assassination attempt on Pope John Paul II's life in May 1981, which is still in use today.Italy's Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni expressed her "personal solidarity" with the Pope as he "faces the ordeal ahead in the coming days".Her sentiments were echoed by Italian President Sergio Mattarella, who offered his "sincerest wishes for a peaceful recovery and a speedy and full return to health".Isaac Herzog, the president of Israel, also wished the pontiff "a full and speedy recovery".The Pope, born Robert Francis Prevost, is the 267th occupant of the throne of St Peter – the first US citizen to do so.He was ordained in 1982 and spent years as a missionary in Peru, where he is remembered as a figure who worked with marginalised communities.During Sunday's service, the Pope confirmed his upcoming visit to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru in November will still go ahead.The Archbishop of Montevideo, Daniel Sturla, said preparations for his tour will continue with "greater enthusiasm" as he called for prayers for his recovery.A lung nodule is a small lump of tissue that is usually detected following an X-ray or CT scan of the chest, according to the NHS.Most nodules do not cause other symptoms.

schema.headline: Pope Leo XIV to have surgery after nodule found on lung

title: Saudi minister vows 'serious response' to Houthi attacks on airports
description: Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after
body: Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they say is a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom. The Yemeni government claimed it was behind that strike, saying it was trying to prevent an unauthorised Iranian plane from landing.Last month, the Houthis launched a surprise offensive along Yemen's south-western Red Sea coast and ousted pro-government forces from areas overlooking the Bab al-Mandab Strait, at the southern end of the Red Sea.They said they posed no threat to international shipping passing through the waterway but that they would continue to target vessels from Saudi Arabia.However, the seizure of the strait contributed to a surge in global oil prices because Saudi Arabia had been relying on the Red Sea for oil exports after the US and Israel's war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.Last week, the Yemeni government announced the start of a new offensive aimed at retaking all territory held by the Houthis.Pro-government forces said they were quickly able to retake areas around Bab al-Mandab with the help of intense Saudi air strikes, but the Houthis denied losing any territory.

schema.headline: Saudi minister vows 'serious response' to Houthi attacks on airports

title: Yandex: Ukraine strikes data centre in third attack on Russian tech giant
description: Yandex confirmed on Telegram that its data centre in Vladimir had been damaged and that operations had been "completely suspended", although it said i
body: Yandex confirmed on Telegram that its data centre in Vladimir had been damaged and that operations had been "completely suspended", although it said it was working to restore connectivity.The other strikes against Yandex facilities were on Thursday in Sasovo and Friday in Kaluga, south-west of Moscow, causing problems for some of its services, such as its AI chatbot and smart home devices.The tech company - which also runs a food-ordering and taxi app used by tens of millions of people - said at the time that its data centres were critical for the normal operation of its services, and that it was "very difficult to predict" when they would be back online.Meanwhile, Russian strikes on Ukraine have continued through the weekend.The State Emergency Service of Ukraine said six people were injured in Russian attacks overnight on four districts in its south-eastern Dnipropetrovsk region.On Saturday, at least 20 people including four children were killed in Russian attacks on Zaporizhzhia, local officials confirmed.Russia has previously also struck Ukrainian data centres, causing internet outages and prompting some firms to move their servers abroad.

schema.headline: Yandex: Ukraine strikes data centre in third attack on Russian tech giant

title: Djibouti boat capsize: Children among 139 dead with 84 still missing, UN says
description: At least 139 migrants including 15 children have died and dozens more are still missing after a boat sank off the coast of Djibouti, the UN's migratio
body: At least 139 migrants including 15 children have died and dozens more are still missing after a boat sank off the coast of Djibouti, the UN's migration office has said.The boat had been travelling from Djibouti to Yemen with 305 people aboard when it capsized near the port town of Obock on Thursday night. Around 82 people were rescued, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) said.IOM's Djibouti mission chief Alexandre Coissac called the tragedy a "stark reminder" of the dangers migrants face when seeking a new life elsewhere.Tens of thousands of migrants from the Horn of Africa make the perilous journey each year hoping to reach Gulf countries for safety and work, the agency says.The organisation revised its toll from 109 on Sunday after 30 more bodies were recovered."This is a devastating loss of life," Coissac said. "Our thoughts are with the survivors and the families who have lost loved ones or remain without news of their relatives."Local authorities are also arranging burials for those who have died, while the survivors - all Ethiopian nationals - have medical care readily available to them.Yemen remains engulfed in a devastating civil war that has lasted more than a decade. Despite this conflict - and growing instability across the wider region - migrants still cross the Bab el-Mandeb Strait to Yemen driven by poverty, insecurity and the growing impacts of climate change.Since 10 September, the IOM said its Displacement Tracking Matrix had observed more than 20,000 "movements" from Ethiopia to Djibouti.

schema.headline: Djibouti boat capsize: Children among 139 dead with 84 still missing, UN says

title: Australia v South Africa: Bad light thwarts Durban Test despite ICC changes
description: Play is already starting at 09:30 local time in Durban. This is the first October Test at Kingsmead, where the sun sets shortly after 18:00 at this ti
body: Play is already starting at 09:30 local time in Durban. This is the first October Test at Kingsmead, where the sun sets shortly after 18:00 at this time of year on South Africa's eastern coast.Still, on day one, play was halted at 15:23 local time after clouds built. Only 65.2 of the scheduled 90 overs had been bowled and the players were unable to return.Day two was slightly better with play continuing until 16:25, but that finish was still 35 minutes earlier than it could have been. Day three's end came at 16:31.On each occasion, the first two sessions have been played in hot, sunny conditions, only for clouds to build in the afternoon - a familiar weather pattern in Durban."Very quickly in the morning, as temperatures have risen inland as the sun heats the ground, a sea breeze has formed with winds coming from the sea into Durban," said BBC weather presenter Chris Fawkes."This has increased humidity levels through the morning and brought some cloud in. As temperatures have started to fall again towards the evening, this has increased the relative humidity with the air getting increasingly saturated."That has caused the cloud to get thicker and lower."One narrative exists that the pink ball moves more under floodlights, though that is not backed up by ball tracking data.Instead, various batters have spoken about the pink ball being more difficult to see. Batting averages are lowest in the evening of day-night matches.Australia have also played in 15 of Test cricket's day-nighters - 10 more than anyone else.Unsurprisingly, the four leading wicket-takers in day-night matches are all Australians. Left-armer Mitchell Starc's haul of 89 wickets in 15 Tests has positioned him as the undisputed pink-ball king.You would not blame teams if they would rather face Australia with the red ball.Former South Africa bowler Vernon Philander said he prefers the idea of switching balls during the match if conditions require it, but that would raise questions over the Test's integrity.Is the potential injustice of one team having to face a pink ball outweighed by the need to get more action of the field?"They have to take it out of the hands of the players completely and enforce it from the umpires' point of view that the pink ball will become in play when the light has faded enough," Philander said."You are always going to have the argument of who is ahead of the game."I would like to see the ICC enforce it on to the officials to make that call."

schema.headline: Australia v South Africa: Bad light thwarts Durban Test despite ICC changes

title: US ranchers wrestle with soaring costs - and their loyalty to Trump
description: Image source, Yvette MannonImage caption, Rancher Yvette Mannon was already dealing with a destructive wildfire and rising fuel costs before the US an
body: Image source, Yvette MannonImage caption, Rancher Yvette Mannon was already dealing with a destructive wildfire and rising fuel costs before the US announced new foreign beef importsBySheila FlynnSenior US reporter, NebraskaNebraska rancher Yvette Mannon was already having a rough year.In April, a wildfire destroyed 1,600 grazing acres and 13 miles (21 km) of fence along the ranch she bought in 2002. The ranch is nestled in a corner of Nebraska that's home to rolling green hills under sweeping Midwestern skies, the landscape dotted with grain silos and feedlots alongside fields and fields of bovines.Mannon's 300 cattle survived the blaze - but the fencing needed to be replaced, and the herd still needed to be fed.With steel prices at their highest levels in years, heavily affected by tariffs imposed by US President Donald Trump, that meant spending $4.89 a foot - for a total exceeding $300,000. On top of that, because so much good grazing land had been destroyed, Mannon also needed a tractor out every day delivering hay to her cattle - at a time when diesel prices, spiking due to the Iran War, were up more than 40% from the previous year.Then in August, the Trump administration announced it would import 300,000 metric tons of duty-free foreign beef in a bid to lower consumer prices. The news hit right before the September-November window when most US calves are weaned and sold.The cattle market tanked immediately.'It felt like a betrayal'"So we're 'Buy American', 'Let's Make America Great'," said Mannon, 63, who voted for Trump. "But for you guys over here, sorry.""It just felt like a betrayal," she said.Many farmers and ranchers across the US say they are being hit from all sides. Recent years have been difficult, with drought affecting crops and already historically low cattle herds. But they say government policies have added to the strain.That has left some in Nebraska, which overwhelmingly backed President Trump during the last election, reassessing their political allegiances. Dan Osborn, an independent candidate running against Trump-backed Republican Pete Ricketts, is performing surprisingly well in the polls ahead of November's Senate race.Republicans seem keenly aware of the discord and frustration among farmers. Both Trump and Nebraska Governor Jim Pillen have in recent weeks announced relief policies aimed at lowering fuel costs for farmers and ranchers, who say they have been struggling for months.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Cattle farming is big business in Nebraska - where ranchers say they are facing soaring costsThe Iran War has sent diesel and fertiliser prices skyrocketing - both daily necessities for agricultural operations. Tariffs have affected machinery costs and repairs, as well as steel and lumber prices. And decisions by the Trump administration - whether it be importing foreign beef or opening up the southern border to Mexican cattle - have sent already-volatile markets into overdrive.Many producers are losing hundreds of dollars per head of cattle."All of this hit cattle markets, as a whole, negatively," said James Mitchell, an assistant professor and agricultural economist at the University of Arkansas.Cattle markets run in 10-12 year cycles, he said, with some good years and some bad. The industry recently enjoyed a particularly lucrative period, where low supply and high demand drove up prices. But now, the market is clearly on a downswing.Jake Wolfinger, 45, has been weathering the downturn at his feedlot near Lexington, Nebraska. He and his wife are both Ohio natives hailing from multi-generational farming families. They moved to Nebraska - which enjoys lush land and the most groundwater in the nation - to strike out on their own.Image source, BBC/Lori PotterImage caption, Jake Wolfinger, 45, says he is frustrated with the way Trump has intervened in the beef marketThe Wolfingers bought a dilapidated feedlot in 2010, which they have turned into a sophisticated operation with 5,500 cattle. Neighbours point to them as an example of what hard work can still do in a tough industry.But Wolfinger did not factor the Iran War, tariffs or foreign beef imports into his planning."Things were just chumming along pretty good," he said, selling cattle for $240 per hundredweight - but that's dropped to $225. That may not seem like much, but it means a loss of potentially hundreds of dollars a head.Wolfinger is also contending with sky-high diesel costs, with some equipment going through 400-gallon tanks a day."It really makes a guy think," he said.A Trump supporter, Wolfinger said he voted for the president because "we needed his spirit in this country". He also expressed frustration with what he called "woke DEI" policies on the left.But he is unhappy with the way the president has intervened in the beef market."People need to stay the hell out of farmers' business, because it's harvest time," Wolfinger said.'People need to stay the hell out of farmers' business'Forty miles northwest, near Callaway, Nebraska, 54-year-old Duane Kimball stands in his shed surrounded by machinery - and a huge Trump banner along one wall."The daily upcharge… is kind of painful," he said."I know a lot of people have had to go back to their banks and increase their lines of credit."Kimball believed the Iran War would have ended long ago.But he does not blame Trump for all of his economic challenges. "To pin that on this administration, I don't think is a fair assessment," he said.He pointed to cumbersome regulations as well as the rising cost of machinery and fertiliser - trends that began before Trump returned to the White House.Image source, BBC/Lori PotterImage caption, "I know a lot of people have had to go back to their banks and increase their lines of credit," said Duane KimballMannon, who returned to her native Nebraska and bought the ranch after a career in banking, believes the agricultural industry will show its feelings at the midterms. But like many around here, she prefers not to engage in too much political debate.That is not a problem for her friend and nearby rancher Jim Jenkins. A former independent senatorial candidate, Jenkins is fiercely proud of Nebraska agriculture and his own ranch, which is on land his family homesteaded more than 150 years ago.Jenkins has been so incensed by the policies he feels are harming Nebraska's agricultural industry that he wrote an opinion article over the summer in an Omaha paper.He has felt the squeeze personally too, citing high diesel, fertiliser, lumber and steel costs - everything from barbed wire to fence posts. That has been compounded by "uncertainty" over what may happen next, he said, and what the next Trump announcement might mean for the industry."Those are the things that keep you up at night," the 69-year-old told BBC News.An outspoken Trump critic who didn't vote for the president during any of his White House bids, Jenkins knows he is an outlier among his conservative neighbours. When Trump was first elected, Jenkins said he hoped he would turn out "to be a practical business guy".Now, he said, "I think he's been anything but practical".Image caption, Jim Jenkins says he is incensed by the policies he feels are harming Nebraska's agricultural industryBut for many Trump-supporting farmers and ranchers, the president's decisions - even when they hit them economically - deserve the benefit of the doubt."We've all known this about Trump. He just kind of could be a little 'shoot, fire, aim,'" Wolfinger said. "I wish you could, you know, put the gun back and holster it and then think about it."But, he said, "I think he's, for the most part, trying to run this country in the right direction".Don Cantrell, whose grandfather started farming family land that now stretches to 12,000 acres, said he is still getting hit on diesel and admits the president "does some stupid things" and "says some stupid things".But Cantrell believes Trump has been the "best president overall". His establishment of DOGE - the Department of Government Efficiency - for example, was exactly what he felt the country needed."Let's cut government waste," he said. "There's so much waste."Image caption, Don Cantrell says he believes Trump has been the "best president overall" - citing his efforts to "cut government waste"Trump also maintains stances on social issues - like abortion and praising Christianity - that align with many Nebraskan voters' personal convictions."I think, in general, if you're conservative in this country, you're going to vote conservative," Wolfinger said.Don Batie, 67, agrees: "There's a lot of other issues besides agriculture."Still, the economic realities are hard to ignore, he said.Batie retired from farming last year for a combination of personal and economic reasons. The corn and soybean farmer watched as prices fell from $7 a bushel for corn in early 2022 to just $4.29 three years later.But costs have not gone down, he said, with tariffs and inflation contributing to his bottom line. As a result, he has had to abandon his longtime dream of passing on the 400-acre farm he owns to his daughter.Image caption, Don Batie, 67, says he has had to abandon his dream of passing on the 400-acre farm he owns to his daughter"It just wasn't going to work now," he said, sitting at the dining room table in the home he grew up in.He only came to that realisation within the past year after crunching the numbers."I knew things hadn't been good," he said. "But when I started working on the numbers… I was like, 'This is going to be bad.'"Batie voted for Trump in 2016 and again in the primary - but not in 2024, because he was disappointed with his policies. He said he had heard similar dissatisfaction throughout the state."They're still strong Republicans," he said of those people."But they're not a Trump supporter anymore."Image source, Lori PotterImage caption, Cattle still need to be bought and sold, and vast ranches - many multi-generational - operate throughout the stateAll over Nebraska, however, the industry soldiers on. On a rainy Thursday in Broken Bow, buyers clad in cowboy hats, plaid shirts and denim gathered for the regular indoor cattle auction.Calves still need to be bought and sold, and ranch operations - many multi-generational - do not pause for politics.Across the train tracks, past feed and hardware stores, Yvette Mannon summed up Nebraskans' resilience and fortitude."People in agriculture are eternal optimists," she said "Otherwise we wouldn't get in it."

schema.headline: US ranchers wrestle with soaring costs - and their loyalty to Trump

title: Watch: Documents falsified to evade tax on Abramovich's wealth
description: Deloitte, the world's biggest accountancy firm, helped in falsifying documents to hide Roman Abramovich's wealth and evade tax, a BBC investigation ha
body: Deloitte, the world's biggest accountancy firm, helped in falsifying documents to hide Roman Abramovich's wealth and evade tax, a BBC investigation has found.BBC Panorama and the Bureau for Investigative Journalism uncovered hundreds of documents that were falsified and backdated to conceal his wealth and evade tax.Roman Abramovich denies any wrongdoing.Watch the investigation into how Abramovich hid his fortune on BBC iPlayer.

schema.headline: Watch: Documents falsified to evade tax on Abramovich's wealth
